title: How to Buy Train Tickets in Uzbekistan
description: Booking the Afrosiyob, the new Khiva high-speed train and the sleepers from Tashkent: the official site, foreign cards, 2026 fares, and what to do when it's sold out.
body_html:
Almost every Uzbekistan itinerary runs on rails. The fast trains out of Tashkent are the easiest way to reach Samarkand, Bukhara and now Khiva. They are cheap by Western standards and comfortable. They are also the part of the trip most likely to go wrong, because the popular departures sell out and the official booking site can be fussy with foreign cards. This guide covers how booking works as of November 2026, what it costs, and how to get a seat when the website says there are none.

The trains you will actually use

Three kinds of train matter to most visitors leaving Tashkent.

  • Afrosiyob: the Spanish-built high-speed train, and the default choice for Samarkand and Bukhara. Tashkent to Samarkand takes about 2 hours 10 minutes to 2 hours 30 minutes depending on the departure, and there are several trains a day. Tashkent to Bukhara takes about four hours.
  • Jaloliddin Manguberdi: the Hyundai Rotem high-speed train that opened on the Tashkent–Khiva line in May 2026. It calls at Samarkand, Bukhara and Urgench and takes about seven and a half to eight and a half hours to reach Khiva, depending on the service. The schedule has changed several times since launch, so check the current days before you plan around it.
  • Sharq and the overnight sleepers: the slower day train (Sharq) takes about three to three and a half hours to Samarkand and costs less, so it is the usual fallback when the Afrosiyob is full. Conventional overnight trains to Khiva take around 14 hours. They offer open bunks (platskart), four-berth compartments (kupe) and two-berth "lux" cabins.

What tickets cost

Uzbekistan Railways raised fares by 15% on 1 February 2026. These are the published one-way Afrosiyob fares since then:

RouteEconomyBusinessVIP
Tashkent–Samarkand311,000 som455,000 som709,000 som
Tashkent–Bukhara509,000 som760,000 som1,138,000 som
Tashkent–Karshi429,000 som642,000 som976,000 som

At the official rate in November 2026 (about 12,000 som to the US dollar) an economy seat to Samarkand is roughly 26 dollars. The Jaloliddin Manguberdi to Khiva launched at 780,000 som one way. Some departures are a little cheaper than the headline fare, so treat these as a guide and check the price shown at booking. See Money & Costs for working with som.

Option 1: the official website and app

The official sales channel is Uzbekistan Railways' e-ticket site, eticket.railway.uz, which has an English version. There is also an official app, listed in the app stores as "Uzrailway tickets". Booking works like this:

  • Create an account first. You can sign up with email or with a Google, Facebook or Telegram login. You can't buy as a guest.
  • Enter passport details for every passenger. Change the document type from the Uzbek passport to a foreign document. Each passport can hold one seat on a given train, so you need every traveller's details, not just your own.
  • Pay. The site now takes foreign Visa and Mastercard through Stripe, which was a real improvement in 2026. Foreign cards are still sometimes declined, so have a second card ready.
  • Keep the e-ticket. You get a ticket with a QR code by email and in your account. Staff scan it from your phone, and you don't need to print it.

Parts of the English interface still show Russian place names. Tashkent's main station may appear as "Toshkent" or with a Russian abbreviation, so read the departure station carefully before you pay.

Option 2: the station ticket office

If the website won't take your card, the ticket offices at the stations sell the same seats. Bring the passport of every traveller you are booking for. Bring som in cash as well, because card acceptance at the counters is inconsistent. Queues can be long in peak season. It is worth going on your first day in Tashkent to buy all your onward tickets in one go rather than the evening before you travel.

Option 3: resellers and agencies

International booking sites such as 12Go sell Afrosiyob and other train tickets, and they take foreign cards reliably. The trade-off is a markup over the official fare. Tashkent travel agencies will also book for you for a fee. Either is a sensible choice if you are booking from abroad and the official site keeps refusing your card. Just don't pay more than a modest premium: the official fares above are the baseline.

When to book, and what to do when it's sold out

Sales open roughly 30 to 45 days before departure. Reports differ on the exact window, so check the site as soon as your dates are fixed. The morning Afrosiyob trains are the first to go, and in spring, autumn and around public holidays they can sell out within hours of release. In late 2026 Uzbek media were still reporting a chronic shortage of seats on domestic routes. Plan for that rather than hoping it improves.

If your train shows as full:

  • Check again. Cancelled seats are released back into the system, often in the last few days before departure and sometimes on the day.
  • Try another class or train. Business class often has seats when economy is gone. A later Afrosiyob or the slower Sharq may get you there with little real loss of time.
  • Change the order of your route. If Tashkent–Bukhara is full, Tashkent–Samarkand followed by Samarkand–Bukhara a day later may not be. This fits naturally into a Silk Road itinerary.
  • Fly one leg. For Khiva in particular, a domestic flight to Urgench is a realistic alternative. A shuttle train links Urgench airport with Khiva in about 42 minutes (25,000 som for adults as of September 2026).

Which Tashkent station?

Tashkent has two main stations. The Afrosiyob and the Jaloliddin Manguberdi to Khiva leave from Tashkent Central, also called Tashkent North (Severny), which has its own metro stop. Many conventional and overnight trains use Tashkent South (Yuzhny) instead. Always go by the station printed on your ticket. A wrong guess means a cross-city taxi against the clock. Getting Around covers taxis to both.

On the day

  • Arrive at least 30 minutes early. Bags go through an X-ray scanner inside the station, and you want time to find your platform.
  • Carry the passport you booked with. Staff check the name on your ticket against your ID before you board.
  • Have the QR code ready on your phone, with a screenshot in case you have no signal.
  • Bring food and water for the longer rides, especially the overnight sleepers.

Is it worth it?

Yes. Once you hold a ticket, Uzbekistan's trains are one of the pleasures of the trip. They are smooth, comfortable and cost a fraction of what comparable trains cost in Europe. The effort is all up front: book early, use the official site if your card cooperates, and keep a fallback ready for the sold-out days. Pair this page with When to Visit, since the busiest travel months are also when tickets are hardest to get.

Frequently asked questions

Can foreigners buy Uzbekistan train tickets online? Yes. The official site, eticket.railway.uz, has an English version and accepts foreign Visa and Mastercard through Stripe, though some cards are still declined. You need an account and the passport details of every passenger.

How far in advance should I book the Afrosiyob? As early as you can. Sales open roughly 30 to 45 days before departure, and morning trains in spring and autumn can sell out within hours.

Do I need to print my train ticket? No. The QR e-ticket on your phone is accepted, but you must also show the passport you booked with.
